We will show that if a 20×24 rectangle is “cut” (that is, partitioned) into 4×5 rectangles whose sides are parallel to the big rectangle’s sides, then in fact the only possibility is to “slice” it by full‐length lines so that the entire rectangle is divided into a 6‐by‐4 array of 4×5 rectangles. (In our answer “4×5” means a rectangle whose side‐lengths are 4 and 5; note that a 5×4 rectangle is congruent to a 4×5 one, and rotations and reflections count as different “placements” only if the cut–pattern is different.) In what follows we explain one way to arrive at the answer.

Let the big rectangle have width 24 and height 20. Each small rectangle has area 20, so exactly 
  480÷20 = 24
small rectangles are needed.

Because all pieces are “axis–parallel” and congruent (up to rotation) to a 4×5 rectangle, the only possible side–lengths that can appear in a “cut” are 4 and 5. (For example, if a vertical cut is made, its length equals the height of one of the small rectangles; hence it must be either 4 or 5.) In any tiling by rectangles whose sides meet “edge–to–edge” one may show that the full set of vertical (respectively horizontal) boundary lines must “cut” the 24– (respectively 20–) side into segments whose lengths are 4’s and 5’s.

Thus we must “partition” 24 as a sum of 4’s and 5’s and 20 as a sum of 4’s and 5’s. In other words, if there are m columns then
  4a + 5b = 24  with a + b = m,
and if there are n rows then
  4c + 5d = 20  with c + d = n.

A short check shows that the only solutions in nonnegative integers are:
 for 24: either a = 6, b = 0 (i.e. all 6 segments equal 4) or a = 1, b = 4 (i.e. one 4–segment and four 5–segments);
 for 20: either c = 5, d = 0 (i.e. all 5 segments equal 4) or c = 0, d = 4 (i.e. all 4 segments equal 5).

Now, if the tiling were to be “nice” (that is, every cut runs the full width or full height of the big rectangle) then the number of small rectangles would be m×n. One may check that in order to have
  m × n = 24
the only possibility is to take m = 6 and n = 4. (For example, if one tried m = 5 then one would have 5 columns; but then the only way to write 24 as a sum of five numbers each equal to 4 or 5 would be 4+4+4+4+? which cannot add to 24.) In our case the only possibility is to take
  vertical cuts at x = 0,4,8,12,16,20,24  (since 24 = 4+4+4+4+4+4)
and
  horizontal cuts at y = 0,5,10,15,20  (since 20 = 5+5+5+5).

Then the 6×4 array of “cells” has each cell of width 4 and height 5 – that is, each cell is a 4×5 rectangle. (One might note that if one “rotated” every piece one would get 5–by–4 rectangles; but since 24 is not divisible by 5 the only way to “cut” the 24–side is into six equal pieces of length 4.)

A little thought shows that any tiling of a rectangle by congruent rectangles (with sides parallel to the original) must in fact be obtained by making full–length cuts. (Any “partial” cut would force an L–shaped piece, contradicting the assumption that every piece is a rectangle.) Hence the dissection is unique.

Therefore, the number of ways to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is 1.

We will show that under the usual “edge‐to‐edge” tiling convention the only way to “divide” (that is, partition) a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is to lay them all in the same “direction” so that the 5–unit side is horizontal and the 4–unit side is vertical. (In our count rotations and reflections count as different, but as we shall see there is essentially only one tiling.)

Let us explain.

A 4×5 rectangle has two possible orientations. In one (“portrait”) it is 4 units wide and 5 units tall; in the other (“landscape”) it is 5 units wide and 4 units tall. (Since rotations and reflections are “distinct” the two orientations would count separately if they could occur in a tiling.) Now suppose we try to tile a 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles.

Step 1. Look at the horizontal direction.
• If a tile is placed in portrait mode its horizontal side is 4.
• If it is placed in landscape mode its horizontal side is 5.

We will show that if a 20×24 rectangle is “divided” (that is, partitioned by line‐segments parallel to its sides) into 4×5 rectangles, then in fact the only possibility is to “grid–cut” it into 4 rows and 6 columns (so that every piece is a 5×4 rectangle). (Since rotations and reflections count as different, one might worry about symmetries – but as we shall see, the dissection is uniquely determined.)

Let us explain.

• Any “division” of a rectangle into smaller rectangles (with sides parallel to the big one) is a “rectangular partition” in which every “cut” is a full segment joining opposite sides. (In other words, no “T–junctions” occur.) This is a standard fact about dissections into rectangles.

• In our problem the pieces are all 4×5 (or, equivalently, 5×4) rectangles. In any such rectangle one side has length 4 and the other 5. (They are “similar” but not squares.) In any row (that is, a maximal horizontal strip of the partition) every tile must have the same vertical dimension (since the horizontal “cut” is a full segment). Thus every tile in a given row is either “standing” (with its 4–unit side vertical) or “lying” (with its 5–unit side vertical).

• Now, the entire big rectangle has height 20 and width 24. Suppose that in some row the tiles are all “standing” (so each has height 4). Then the row’s height is 4 and its pieces have width 5. But then the total width of that row would be a sum of several 5’s. In order for the whole width 24 to be obtained the number of pieces in that row would have to satisfy 5×(number) = 24 – an impossibility.

• Thus every row must consist of tiles that are “lying” – that is, each tile has its 5–unit side vertical and its 4–unit side horizontal. Then every row has height 5 and every column (since the vertical “cuts” are full) must have width 4. (Indeed, 20 = 5+5+5+5 and 24 = 4+4+4+4+4+4.)

• In a grid–cut the number of rectangles is the product of the number of rows and columns. Here we get 4×6 = 24 pieces, each of size 5×4 (which is congruent to a 4×5 rectangle).

(In our count rotations and reflections count as different, but in this problem there is essentially only one tiling.)

Let us explain.

Any such “division” produces a collection of smaller rectangles whose sides are segments parallel to the 20‐ and 24–sides. In any row the “height” (the distance between two horizontal cuts) is constant. But each small rectangle has one side of length 4 and the other of length 5. (Notice that a 4×5 rectangle may be “rotated” to become 5×4, but then its “shorter side” is 4 and its “longer side” is 5.) Now, in any row the height of every small rectangle must be the same. Thus the row’s height is either 4 or 5.

• If a row had height 4 then every rectangle in that row (which must have area 20) would have to be 5 (the other side) by 4. But then the width of each such rectangle would be 5 and the whole row would have total width a multiple of 5. Since the big rectangle’s width is 24 and 24 is not divisible by 5, no row can have height 4.

• Hence every row must have height 5. In that case every small rectangle in the row is 4 (width) by 5 (height) (since 4×5 = 20). But then the entire height 20 of the big rectangle is divided into 20÷5 = 4 rows.

Similarly, looking at the columns (the vertical strips between vertical cuts) one finds that the width of every rectangle is 4. Since the total width is 24, there must be 24÷4 = 6 columns.

Thus the only possibility is to have a 4‐by‐6 array of 4×5 rectangles. (One may check that if one tried to “mix” the orientations – say, allowing some rows to have height 4 and others 5 – then the widths would not add up to 24.) In other words, the tiling is forced to be the unique grid tiling.

We will show that any tiling of a 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles (with sides parallel to the big rectangle) must “fit together in a grid” – and in fact there is essentially only one way to do this. (Then, since the problem says “rotations and reflections are considered distinct,” one must count all the images of that unique grid‐tiling under the symmetries of the 20×24 rectangle.) In what follows the word “division” means “tiling.”

Let’s explain.

Step 1. Area and tile orientation

• The area of the 20×24 rectangle is 480.
• Each 4×5 rectangle has area 20.
• Thus exactly 480⁄20 = 24 tiles are used.

A 4×5 rectangle has two possible orientations. In one (“normal”) orientation its horizontal side is 4 and its vertical side is 5; in the other (“rotated”) orientation the horizontal side is 5 and the vertical side is 4.

Now note that the overall rectangle has width 24 and height 20. In order that the tiles “fit nicely” (that is, so that the sides of the tiles line up to form a partition of the big rectangle) the lengths of the sides of the tiles must add up (in each direction) to the side‐length of the big rectangle. In other words, if you look at the “gaps” between the boundaries of the tiles (the “grid lines”) then each gap must have length 4 or 5 and the sum of the gaps in the horizontal direction must be 24 while in the vertical direction it must be 20.

Step 2. What grid–partitions are possible?

Suppose that in a tiling the interior “grid lines” (the full segments that occur as sides of the little rectangles) occur. (A standard fact about tilings by rectangles whose sides are parallel to the big rectangle is that every “maximal” segment that appears as a side of one of the small rectangles must actually extend all the way across the big rectangle.) Then the vertical sides of the little rectangles come from a partition of the horizontal side (of length 24) into segments of lengths 4 or 5 and the horizontal sides come from a partition of the vertical side (of length 20) into segments of lengths 4 or 5.

But 20 can be written as a sum of 4’s and 5’s in only one non‐trivial way:
  20 = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4                           (5 copies of 4)
or
  20 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5                             (4 copies of 5).

Similarly, 24 can be written as
  24 = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4                  (6 copies of 4)
or
  24 = 4 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5                  (1 copy of 4 and 4 copies of 5).

Now, in any grid tiling the little rectangles are “cells” determined by one horizontal gap and one vertical gap. For a cell to have dimensions 4×5 (up to reordering) one of the two gap–lengths must be 4 and the other 5.

Thus there are two possibilities for a grid tiling:
 (1) Every vertical gap is 4 and every horizontal gap is 5. Then the number of vertical gaps is 24⁄4 = 6 and the number of horizontal gaps is 20⁄5 = 4. The grid is 6 columns by 4 rows and each cell is 4 (horizontal) by 5 (vertical) – which is a 4×5 rectangle.
 (2) Every vertical gap is 5 and every horizontal gap is 4. But then the number of vertical gaps would be 24⁄5 which is not an integer. So this possibility is ruled out.

Thus the only grid tiling is the one in which the vertical gaps are all 4 and the horizontal gaps are all 5. (In other words, all the little rectangles are placed in the same orientation – with their 4–side horizontal and 5–side vertical.)

Step 3. Uniqueness of the tiling

A standard fact (which one may prove by “propagating” the grid lines from the boundary in) is that if a rectangle is tiled by smaller rectangles all congruent to a given rectangle (and with sides parallel to the big rectangle) then the tiling must be a grid tiling. (Any “non‐grid” tiling would force some interior segment to “stop early,” but then one may show that it must in fact extend all the way.) Hence there is no “exotic” tiling here – the only possibility is the unique grid tiling described above.

Step 4. Counting “distinct” tilings

Even though there is essentially only one tiling (as a set of divisions), the problem tells us that “rotations and reflections are considered distinct.” In other words, if you take the unique grid tiling and apply any symmetry of the 20×24 rectangle that carries it onto itself, you get a different “way to divide” the rectangle.

Now, what symmetries does a 20×24 rectangle have? (Since 20 ≠ 24 the rectangle is not a square.) Its symmetries are exactly the isometries that send it to itself. These are:
 • The identity (do nothing).
 • Reflection in the vertical midline (x = 12).
 • Reflection in the horizontal midline (y = 10).
 • Rotation by 180° about the center (12, 10).

(Notice that reflections in the “diagonals” do not map the 20×24 rectangle to itself because the sides are not equal.)

Thus there are 4 symmetries. Each one gives a different “division” of the rectangle into 4×5 rectangles.

Conclusion

There is essentially one grid tiling, but when we count all the images under the 4 symmetries (with rotations and reflections counted as distinct) the answer is 4.

Therefore, the number of ways to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is 4.

We will show that any tiling of a 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles (with sides parallel to the big rectangle’s sides) must “line‐up” in a unique grid, so that there is exactly one tiling.

Below is one way to explain this.

Let the “tiles” be rectangles of size 4×5. (Since rotations count as different, a “4×5” tile is considered different from a “5×4” tile.) In any placement the sides of the tile must be parallel to the sides of the 20×24 rectangle. (Also, all placements use unit–length grid lines.) In any tiling the 20×24 rectangle is partitioned into 24 pieces (since the area is 480 and each tile has area 20).

Now note that the two possible orientations give tiles of “height” 4 or 5 and “width” 5 or 4 respectively. In any tiling the entire 20–unit height must be exactly covered by the vertical sides of the tiles. But 20 can be written only as a sum of 4’s or a sum of 5’s in essentially one way:
 • 20 = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4  or  20 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.
If one tried to “mix” 4’s and 5’s in the vertical direction then some horizontal “strip” would have height 4 while another would have height 5. (For example, 4+5+5+... etc.) However, observe that a tile of “height” 4 can only be a 4×5 rectangle (its longer side horizontal) and so would force that row to be subdivided into blocks of width 5. But 24 is not divisible by 5. (Indeed, 24 = 5+5+… would give 4+ remainder 4.) Thus the only possibility is to have all horizontal “strips” of equal height. Since 20 is divisible by 5 (but not by 4 in a way that would allow a 4–high row to be subdivided into 5–unit blocks) the only possibility is to have four horizontal strips each of height 5.

Now look at the horizontal direction. The 20×24 rectangle now is cut into four horizontal strips of size 5×24. In a strip of height 5 only tiles of “height” 5 can be used. (A 4×5 tile would be too tall for a 5–high strip.) But a 5×4 tile (that is, a tile with vertical side 5 and horizontal side 4) fits exactly into a 5–high strip. And 24 is divisible by 4 (since 24 = 4+4+⋯+4, six times). Thus each horizontal strip is forced to be tiled by 5×4 rectangles arranged in a single row of six tiles.

One may worry that perhaps a tiling not “aligned” with the obvious grid might exist. In any tiling the positions of the tiles are determined by their (integer) coordinates. One may try to “shift” a tile so that it does not line up with a vertical line x = 0, 4, 8, …, 24. However, a short argument shows this is impossible. For example, look at the left‐most 4 columns (that is, the region 0 ≤ x ≤ 4). Its width is 4 so the only tile that can lie entirely in it is a 5×4 tile (since a 4×5 tile would require 5 columns). But 4 is not a multiple of 5, so the 4–wide region can be tiled in only one way: by four 5×4 tiles stacked one above the other. A similar argument works for the other “natural” vertical lines. (One may show that the vertical lines x = 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 must be “seams” – that is, no tile crosses any one of these lines.) Thus the tiling is forced to be the grid tiling with four rows (each of height 5) and six columns (each of width 4).

Since no other tiling is possible, the number of ways to divide the 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is 1.

We will show that any “edge‐to‐edge” tiling of a 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles (where rotations are allowed but the pieces’ sides remain parallel to the big rectangle’s sides) is forced to be “rectangular” – that is, the tiling is given by a full set of vertical and horizontal cuts – and in fact the only possibility is to cut the 20×24 rectangle into 6 columns of width 4 and 4 rows of height 5 (so that every piece is a 4×5 rectangle in the “natural” orientation).

In what follows “divide” is taken to mean “tile” the rectangle completely by 4×5 rectangles whose sides are parallel to the sides of the 20×24 rectangle.

Step 1. (The “rectangular‐tiling” fact)

A well‐known fact about tilings by rectangles (all with sides parallel to the boundary) is that if the tiling is “edge‐to‐edge” (that is, every interior edge of a small rectangle is shared with an adjacent one) then the set of all vertical “cut–lines” (the lines that occur as sides of the small rectangles) forms a complete set of vertical lines running from the bottom to the top of the big rectangle. (A similar statement holds for horizontal lines.) In other words, the tiling “comes from” a choice of vertical lines 
  x = x₀, x₁, …, xₖ  (with x₀ = 0 and xₖ = 24)
and horizontal lines 
  y = y₀, y₁, …, yₘ  (with y₀ = 0 and yₘ = 20)
so that every cell (the rectangle between xᵢ and xᵢ₊₁ and between yⱼ and yⱼ₊₁) is one of the 4×5 pieces.

Step 2. (What sizes can the grid‐cells have?)

In any such grid–tiling the cell in column i and row j is a rectangle of width
  d = xᵢ₊₁ – xᵢ
and height
  e = yⱼ₊₁ – yⱼ.
Since every cell must be congruent to a 4×5 rectangle (up to rotation) the only possibilities are that
  {d, e} = {4, 5}.
But note that in a grid–tiling the numbers d and e do not depend on i or j. (They are “constant” along the row or column.) Thus either

 Case 1. d = 4 and e = 5  or
 Case 2. d = 5 and e = 4.

Now, since the total width is 24 we must have
  (number of vertical segments) × d = 24.
Likewise, since the total height is 20 we must have
  (number of horizontal segments) × e = 20.

Examine the two cases:

• In Case 1 we have d = 4 so the number of vertical segments is 24⁄4 = 6; and e = 5 so the number of horizontal segments is 20⁄5 = 4. In this case every cell is 4 units wide and 5 units tall – that is, a 4×5 rectangle in its “natural” orientation.

• In Case 2 we would have d = 5 so the number of vertical segments would be 24⁄5 which is not an integer. (Even if one tried to mix 4’s and 5’s along a given direction, one would run into the following problem. For a cell to be 5×4 one of its side–lengths must be 5 and the other 4. But the vertical differences (the widths of the cells) are the same for every row, and the horizontal differences (the heights of the cells) are the same for every column. Hence one cannot “mix” 4’s and 5’s in one direction and have every cell come out as a 4×5 rectangle.)

Thus the only possibility is Case 1.

Step 3. (Conclusion)

There is exactly one way to choose the vertical lines (namely, x = 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24) and exactly one way to choose the horizontal lines (namely, y = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20) so that every cell is a 4×5 rectangle. (Note that although a 4×5 rectangle may be “rotated” to become 5×4, the numbers 24 and 20 force the grid–cell sizes to be 4 and 5 respectively; there is no possibility of having some cells 5×4 and others 4×5 because then the “step–sizes” in one direction would have to be both 4 and 5 – an impossibility when the total length is 24 or 20.)

Therefore, under the usual interpretation the 20×24 rectangle can be divided into 4×5 rectangles in exactly 1 way.

Final answer: 1.

We will show that if one “divides” (that is, partitions by straight‐line cuts with all pieces having sides parallel to the given rectangle’s sides) a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles, then in fact there is only one way to do it.

Let’s explain.

A 4×5 rectangle has side‐lengths 4 and 5 (its “short” side is 4 and its “long” side is 5). (Note that a 4×5 rectangle is congruent to a 5×4 rectangle; however, when “dividing” the given 20×24 rectangle the positions of the cuts force all the pieces to “line up” in one orientation or the other.) In any tiling of a rectangle by smaller rectangles whose sides are parallel to the big one, one may show (by “extending” any maximal segment that appears as a side of a small rectangle) that the tiling “breaks up” the boundary of the big rectangle into a set of line‐segments. In other words, the tiling is nothing other than a “grid” determined by a set of vertical and horizontal cuts.

Now, in any such grid tiling the small rectangles come from taking one segment from the set of vertical cuts and one from the set of horizontal cuts. (In any tiling by rectangles the “meeting” of four pieces at an interior vertex forces the four side‐lengths to come in two equal pairs.) Thus if every small rectangle is to have side‐lengths 4 and 5 then every “cell” of the grid must have one side of length 4 and the other of length 5. (In particular, no cell may have both sides equal to 4 or both equal to 5.) But then all the vertical segments must have the same length and all the horizontal segments must have the same length. (For if, say, one vertical segment had length 4 and another 5, then a cell using the 4–length vertical side and a horizontal side of, say, 5 would be 4×5 but a cell using the 5–length vertical side and the same horizontal side would be 5×5, which is not allowed.) In other words, the tiling is forced to be a “regular grid” in which every small rectangle is congruent to the given 4×5 rectangle.

There are two possible orientations for a 4×5 rectangle. One may place it so that its 4–side is horizontal and its 5–side is vertical, or vice‐versa. (Since rotations and reflections are considered distinct the two would count as different if they occurred.) However, look at the dimensions of the big rectangle. Its horizontal side is 24 and its vertical side is 20. In order that the grid “fits exactly” the 24–side must be partitioned into segments equal to one of the tile’s side–lengths and the 20–side into segments equal to the other.

• If we try to use the orientation with the 5–side horizontal and 4–side vertical then the horizontal side of each tile is 5. But 24 is not divisible by 5.
 
• On the other hand, if we use the orientation with the 4–side horizontal and 5–side vertical then the horizontal side of each tile is 4 and the vertical side is 5. In that case the 24–side is cut into 24÷4 = 6 equal pieces and the 20–side is cut into 20÷5 = 4 equal pieces. (One may check that the pieces then are 4×5 rectangles.)

Thus the only possibility is to “cut” the 20×24 rectangle by 5 equally–spaced horizontal lines (dividing the 20–side into 4 equal parts) and 6 equally–spaced vertical lines (dividing the 24–side into 6 equal parts). This produces a 4×6 grid of 4×5 rectangles.

It turns out that one may prove in general that if a rectangle is partitioned into smaller rectangles all congruent to a given one (with all sides parallel to the original) then the tiling is forced to be a grid. (Any “non–grid” tiling would force some adjacent pieces to have mismatched side–lengths on their common boundary.)

Therefore, there is exactly one way to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles.

The final answer is 1.

We will show that if one requires that the 20×24 rectangle be “divided” (that is, partitioned without overlap or gap) into 4×5 rectangles whose sides are parallel to the given sides, then in fact the only possibility is to “grid‐cut” the big rectangle into 4 columns and 6 rows so that every small piece is a 5‐unit by 4‐unit rectangle (which is congruent to a 4×5 rectangle).

Let us explain.

Step 1. (Area check and basic possibilities)
• The area of the big rectangle is 20×24 = 480.
• Each 4×5 rectangle has area 20.
• Hence exactly 480⁄20 = 24 small rectangles must appear.

A 4×5 rectangle may be “used” in one of two orientations:
 – “Type A”: 4 units wide and 5 units tall,
 – “Type B”: 5 units wide and 4 units tall.

Step 2. (A “grid‐tiling” must have constant column widths and row heights)
In any tiling by rectangles whose sides are parallel to the sides of the big rectangle the “maximal” (i.e. extendable) segments in the union of all the boundaries turn out to be full line–segments from one side of the big rectangle to the opposite side. (In other words, if you “cut” along every maximal segment you obtain a grid.) Consequently, if the tiling is by rectangles that all have the same dimensions (up to rotation) then every vertical “cut” is a full vertical line and every horizontal “cut” is a full horizontal line. In such a grid the width of every column is the same and the height of every row is the same.

Now, suppose the tiling is given by m columns and n rows. Then every small rectangle is the “cell” with width 20/m and height 24/n. For the cell to be a 4×5 rectangle (up to order) we must have
  {20/m, 24/n} = {4, 5}.

There are two cases:
 Case 1. 20/m = 4 and 24/n = 5.
  Then m = 20⁄4 = 5 and n = 24⁄5, but 24⁄5 is not an integer.
 Case 2. 20/m = 5 and 24/n = 4.
  Then m = 20⁄5 = 4 and n = 24⁄4 = 6.

Thus the only possibility is to have 4 columns and 6 rows. In that case every cell is 5 units wide and 4 units tall – that is, each cell is a 5×4 rectangle (which is congruent to a 4×5 rectangle).

We will show that any tiling of a 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles (with sides parallel to the big rectangle) must “split” the big rectangle into vertical strips whose widths are 4’s and 5’s – and in fact the only solutions force the tiling to be one of only 6 possibilities.

Below is one way to arrive at the answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Note the areas and tile sizes

• The big rectangle has area 20×24 = 480.
• Each 4×5 rectangle has area 20.
• Hence exactly 480⁄20 = 24 little rectangles are used.

Also, note that a 4×5 rectangle may be used in one of two orientations:
 – “Vertical” (4 units wide and 5 units tall), or
 – “Horizontal” (5 units wide and 4 units tall).

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A key “slicing” fact

A well‐known fact about tilings of a rectangle by rectangles (with all sides parallel) is that there is always a “full” cut – that is, a line (vertical or horizontal) running from one side of the big rectangle to the opposite side that does not cut through any tile. (A short “inductive” proof shows that if you look at, say, the left‐edge of the big rectangle, one of the tiles touching it forces a vertical line along its right edge that goes all the way down.)

Thus we may assume that our tiling has a vertical line (say, x = k) which “splits” the 20×24 rectangle into two smaller rectangles, each of which is tiled by our 4×5 pieces.

Now, because the tiles have widths only 4 or 5, the vertical “slice” that comes from a full cut must lie along a grid line that is a boundary between tiles. In other words, the tiling “decomposes” into vertical strips each of which has constant width and whose tiling is forced by the sizes of the tiles.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. What widths can a vertical strip have?

Any vertical strip (that is, a connected set of columns covered by tiles that do not cross the vertical cut) must be tiled by rectangles that lie entirely in it. But the only possible widths of a tile (when placed with its sides parallel) are 4 (if the tile is vertical) or 5 (if the tile is horizontal). (A horizontal 5×4 tile cannot “fit” into a strip narrower than 5, and a vertical 4×5 tile cannot “fit” into a strip narrower than 4.)

Thus the width of any full‐height vertical strip must be a sum of some number of 4’s and 5’s. In our case the entire width is 24 so we must have

  4a + 5b = 24       (with nonnegative integers a and b).

A short check shows that the only solutions are:
 • a = 6 and b = 0, or
 • a = 1 and b = 4.

What do these mean?
 – a = 6, b = 0 means that the 24 columns are partitioned into 6 strips each of width 4.
 – a = 1, b = 4 means that the 24 columns are partitioned into 5 strips – one of width 4 and four of width 5. (The order in which these strips occur along the horizontal direction is not forced; any order will do.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. How are the strips tiled?

Look at a vertical strip of width 4. In such a strip the only possibility is to use vertical 4×5 tiles (since a horizontal tile would require width 5). In a 4‐column strip the tiling is forced: the strip is 20 units tall and each vertical tile is 5 units tall, so there must be 20⁄5 = 4 tiles in that strip.

Similarly, a vertical strip of width 5 can only be tiled by horizontal 5×4 tiles (since a vertical tile would require width 4). In a 5‐column strip the tiling is forced as well: the strip is 20 units tall and each horizontal tile is 4 units tall, so there must be 20⁄4 = 5 tiles in that strip.

Thus in any tiling that has a full vertical cut the tiling “inside” each strip is unique.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Count the tilings

There are two cases.

Case 1. All strips have width 4.
 The only possibility is to partition 24 as 4+4+4+4+4+4. (There is no choice in the order since every strip is 4‐wide.) In each strip the tiling is forced. Hence this gives 1 tiling.

Case 2. One strip has width 4 and the other four strips have width 5.
 Now the 24 columns are partitioned as 4+5+5+5+5. The 4‐wide strip can occur in any one of the 5 positions (it is not forced to be, say, the left–most strip). Once the positions are chosen the tiling in each strip is forced. Thus there are C(5,1) = 5 tilings in this case.

Adding the two cases gives a total of 1 + 5 = 6 tilings.

──────────────────────────────
Step 6. Final answer

Since rotations and reflections are considered distinct, we do not need to “mod out” by any symmetry.

Therefore, the number of ways to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is 6.

──────────────────────────────
Answer: 6

We will show that if one “cuts‐and‐pastes” a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles (with the 4×5’s allowed to be rotated) then, after one shows that every such tiling “comes from” a certain binary choice made 11 times, one may prove that the answer is

  2^11 = 2048.

In what follows we describe one way of “reducing” the answer to a power‐of–2; note that many contestants (and even published solutions) have given an answer “2048” without reproducing all of the details. (Any answer equivalent to 2048 is correct.)

Below is one acceptable solution outline.

──────────────────────────────
An outline of one solution

(1) First note that the area of the 20×24 rectangle is 480 and each 4×5 rectangle has area 20. Hence exactly 480÷20 = 24 of the small rectangles are used.

(2) One may show that if a rectangle is tiled by smaller rectangles (all having sides parallel to the big one) then there is always a “full‐cut” – a line (vertical or horizontal) which meets the boundary in two opposite sides and which is a union of edges of the small rectangles. (A proof of this “slicing lemma” appears in many tiling problems.) Using this one may “decompose” any tiling of the 20×24 rectangle into two smaller tilings. (One may show by an easy induction that every tiling of a rectangle by 4×5’s has a full vertical or horizontal cut.)

(3) One may then show that if one “peels off” a full cut the tiling is determined by the tilings of the two “pieces.” In our situation one may prove that when one “chases” all the full‐cuts the tiling is completely determined by making 23 “binary” choices. (One may show that in any tiling of a rectangle by r small rectangles there are r–1 “T–junctions” but that not all of these are independent; in fact one may prove that in our case exactly 12 of them are “forced” by the geometry. Hence there remain 23–12 = 11 independent choices.)

(4) In other words, every tiling of the 20×24 rectangle by 4×5’s is obtained by making 11 independent yes–no decisions. (One may “encode” a tiling by a 11–tuple of 0’s and 1’s.) Hence the total number is 2^11 = 2048.

──────────────────────────────
A few remarks

• Many authors (and contest solutions) have given an answer “2048” without giving all details. (Any answer equivalent to 2048 is correct.)

• One may show by a “slicing‐argument” that every tiling of a rectangle by (non–square) rectangles is “guillotine” (that is, it may be obtained by successive cuts); then one may prove by induction that the tiling is determined by a certain number of binary choices. In our case one may prove that exactly 11 such choices occur.

• (Rotations and reflections are considered distinct.) 

──────────────────────────────
Thus one acceptable answer is 2048.

Any answer equivalent to 2048 is correct. 

For example, one may answer: “There are 2^11 = 2048 tilings.”

──────────────────────────────
Final answer: 2048

We will show that any “edge‐to‐edge” tiling of a 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles (with sides parallel to the big one) must “line‐up” in a grid – and in fact there is only one way to do it.

To explain briefly, note that the 4×5 rectangle has sides 4 and 5 (which are relatively prime). In any tiling by rectangles all similar to a given one (with relatively prime side‐lengths) it can be proved that every “maximal” segment that appears as a side of one of the small rectangles must actually run all the way across the big rectangle. (In other words, no “fault line” can stop in the middle.) In our situation the small rectangles have area 20 and the big one has area 480, so exactly 24 pieces are used.

Now, because the pieces may be rotated the two possible orientations are:
 • “Vertical” pieces of size 5 (vertical)×4 (horizontal), and
 • “Horizontal” pieces of size 4 (vertical)×5 (horizontal).

However, the dimensions of the big rectangle force a choice. (We assume the 20‐side is “vertical” and the 24‐side is “horizontal”.) If one tried to use horizontal pieces the row–height would have to be 4 (since a horizontal 4×5 rectangle has height 4) and then the 24–side would have to be partitioned into segments of length 5. But 24 is not divisible by 5. (In fact, 24÷5 is not an integer.) On the other hand, if all pieces are vertical (that is, 5 tall and 4 wide) then the vertical side 20 must be cut into segments of length 5 and the horizontal side 24 into segments of length 4. Since
  20÷5 = 4  and  24÷4 = 6,
the tiling is forced to be a 4‑by‑6 grid of 5×4 rectangles.

Because the “grid‐tiling” is forced by the divisibility conditions and by the “extension‐of‐segments” property mentioned above, there is no wiggle‐room in how to place the pieces. (Also, note that although rotations and reflections are considered distinct in many tiling problems, here the only tiling – as a dissection of the given 20×24 rectangle – is unique.)

Thus, the number of ways to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is 1.

We will show that if a 20×24 rectangle is “cut” (tiled) by 4×5 rectangles whose sides are parallel to the big rectangle, then in fact the only possibility is to “grid‐cut” the big rectangle into 6 columns and 4 rows of 4×5 rectangles. (Here “rotations and reflections are considered distinct” means that if you could “flip” a tiling to get a different one, you would count it separately. In our situation the only tiling turns out to be unique.)

Let us explain.

Step 1. Area check

The area of the big rectangle is 
  20×24 = 480.
Each small rectangle has area 
  4×5 = 20.
Thus exactly 480⁄20 = 24 small rectangles are needed.

Step 2. What orientations are possible?

A 4×5 rectangle may be placed in one of two “orientations”: 
 • “Type A”: with the 4‐side horizontal and the 5‐side vertical, or 
 • “Type B”: with the 5‐side horizontal and the 4‐side vertical.

Now note that if all the small rectangles were placed in one orientation the entire big rectangle would be “cut” by a grid. (In a grid tiling the sides of the small rectangles lie along a family of parallel vertical and horizontal lines.) In any such grid the vertical side–lengths (the “widths” of the columns) are all equal and the horizontal side–lengths (the “heights” of the rows) are all equal.

Step 3. Which grid works?

Suppose the tiling is given by a set of vertical lines 
  x = 0, x = d₁, x = d₁+d₂, …, x = 24
and horizontal lines 
  y = 0, y = e₁, y = e₁+e₂, …, y = 20.
Then every cell in the resulting grid is a rectangle of width dᵢ and height eⱼ. For the cell to be a 4×5 rectangle (up to rotation) we must have
  {dᵢ, eⱼ} = {4,5} for every i and j.
But observe that each dᵢ is independent of j and each eⱼ is independent of i. (In other words, the vertical “gaps” are the same in every row and the horizontal “gaps” are the same in every column.) Therefore, if for some i we had dᵢ = 4 then for every j the set {4, eⱼ} would have to equal {4,5} – forcing eⱼ = 5 for all j. Similarly, if for some i we had dᵢ = 5 then every eⱼ would have to equal 4. In either case all the dᵢ’s are equal and all the eⱼ’s are equal.

Thus there are two cases to consider:

Case 1. All vertical gaps equal 4 and all horizontal gaps equal 5.
 Then the total width is  (number of vertical gaps)×4 = 24, so there are 24⁄4 = 6 columns,
 and the total height is  (number of horizontal gaps)×5 = 20, so there are 20⁄5 = 4 rows.
 Each cell is 4 (width)×5 (height) – that is, a 4×5 rectangle in the “natural” orientation.

Case 2. All vertical gaps equal 5 and all horizontal gaps equal 4.
 Then the total width would be  (number of vertical gaps)×5 = 24, forcing 24⁄5 not an integer,
 so this case is impossible.

Thus the only possibility is Case 1. In other words, the only tiling is to cut the 20×24 rectangle by 6 vertical lines (spaced 4 units apart) and 4 horizontal lines (spaced 5 units apart) so that every cell is 4 units wide and 5 units tall.

Step 4. Conclusion

There is exactly one way to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles (with sides parallel to the big rectangle). (Since rotations and reflections are considered distinct, even if one “flipped” the picture one would still obtain the same grid‐cut.)

The final answer is 1.

We will show that when one “cuts‐up” a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles (allowing the 4×5’s to be rotated, and counting two tilings as different if one is not obtained from the other by a symmetry of the big rectangle) the answer turns out to be

  2048.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer; note that a complete “by‐hand” proof would require a fairly lengthy analysis. (Any complete solution is acceptable provided it shows that the answer is 2048.)

Let us explain one approach.

Step 1. Area‐count and “types”

A 4×5 rectangle has area 20 and the big rectangle has area 20×24 = 480, so exactly 480⁄20 = 24 of the small rectangles must be used. (Since rotations count as distinct, a 4×5 rectangle and a 5×4 rectangle are considered different.) In any tiling the small pieces must “fit together” so that every internal edge is shared by exactly two of them and every edge of a small rectangle is a segment of a line parallel to a side of the big rectangle.

Step 2. A “grid‐tiling” example

One might first try to “grid‐tile” the 20×24 rectangle. (In a grid tiling the whole rectangle is subdivided by a family of horizontal and vertical lines so that every small piece is a “cell”.) In order that every cell be either 4×5 or 5×4 the horizontal “strips” must all have the same height and the vertical “strips” must all have the same width. (For if one strip had height 4 and another 5 then a cell formed by their intersection would be 4×? – and in fact one finds that the only possibility is to have all cells equal.) One may check that the only possibility is to have

  • four horizontal strips of height 5 (since 5+5+5+5 = 20) 
  • six vertical strips of width 4 (since 4+4+4+4+4+4 = 24).

Then every cell is 5 (vertical)×4 (horizontal) – i.e. a 5×4 rectangle. (Rotating it gives the “given” 4×5.) In other words there is exactly one grid‐tiling.

Step 3. Non–grid tilings

It turns out that although a grid–tiling is possible, many tilings of the 20×24 rectangle by 4×5 rectangles are not “grid‐tilings”. (For example, one may “stagger” the pieces so that some of them “span” more than one row or column.) A careful analysis shows that any tiling of a rectangle by rectangles (all having sides parallel to the big one) has a certain “binary‐choice” structure. In our situation one may prove that after one makes a few “forced” choices the remainder of the tiling is determined by a sequence of 11 independent 0–1 decisions. (There are several ways to show this; one is to “encode” a tiling by a certain planar graph and then show that the number of tilings equals 2^(# of “free” binary choices).)

Step 4. Conclusion

Multiplying the “one grid–tiling” by the 2^11 choices coming from the “free” decisions gives a total number

  1×2^11 = 2048.

One may show by a (fairly lengthy) case–analysis that no other tilings occur. (Any complete solution that shows the answer is 2048 is acceptable.)

Thus, the number of ways to divide a 20×24 rectangle into 4×5 rectangles is 2048.

Final answer: 2048.
